# Patterns for Freya phone agents

What worked and what failed on the platform. Each item is general: it holds for any brief of this kind of call.
The kit documents (`$KIT/docs/*.md`) are the source of the platform facts. This file adds the design.

## The shape of a call

A collections-style call has stages. Give each stage its own node, so that each prompt is short and each exit is a
route that code can check:

1. `setup` (code, the initial node, passthrough): compute every date fact from the call variable `now` (never the
   real clock): today, the weekday, business days ahead, week ends, callback windows. Write them as text variables
   that the prompts show (`{{today_facts}}`), and as plain values that later code reads.
2. `opening` (conversation): the first sentence as a fixed line (`on_enter` type `tts`, with `{{title}} {{last_name}}`
   style variables). Find out who is on the line. Extract an enum (for example `who`: customer, someone_else,
   wrong_number, deceased, refuses, unclear) and route on it with `equals`. Never route on a free intent when an enum
   can carry it.
3. `someone_else` and other early exits (conversation): what the brief allows to tell a third party, and a callback
   if the brief has one. Nothing about the account.
4. `identity` (conversation): ask the security questions one at a time, call the verify tool after EACH answer,
   also when the same message holds a question or a complaint ("1990. How much do I owe?"): check the answer first,
   then reply. Seen in a test: the model answered the question, skipped the check of a wrong answer, and so gave the
   customer one more try than the brief allows. Never judge an answer yourself: only the tool result counts. The
   result hook says what the answer means (passed, wrong with N left, hint such as a swapped day and month, all
   passed). Route on the tool's result variables: all passed, check ended, refused.
5. `load_account` (api_request, passthrough): the account tool in `pre_actions`, `response_mapping` on the node.
6. `account_facts` (code, passthrough): per product, everything the brief computes: the name in words, the amount
   as speech, the band, the deadline, the floor, the number of attempts, the allowed promise dates. Write one text
   block for the prompt (`{{account_facts}}`) and plain values for code. Put the product ids in the text: the model
   must copy them, never invent them.
7. `negotiate` (conversation): the debt statement, the ask, the attempts, the read-back, the write tools. The prompt
   carries the brief's rules for this stage in order, and the facts block.
8. `close`: one `close_call`-style tool call that is the last tool call, then an `end_call` node. Route to the
   `end_call` node on the close tool's success counter or result.

Merge or split stages when the brief needs it. A stage with strict rules of its own gets its own node.

## How customers talk

The scored customers talk like people: they give a number in two parts, correct themselves, say amounts and dates in
words, ask back, and talk about other things. Write these rules into the prompts of every node that collects a value:

- Never call a check tool (identity, verification) with a partial value. A wrong-looking answer costs the customer
  one of the allowed tries. Call it only when the value is complete in the form that the tool API describes (for
  example all four digits, a full date with the year). Write this into the tool description and the node prompt.
- A partial value: keep the part that the customer gave and ask only for the missing part ("And the year?"). Do not
  ask for the whole value again: a customer who talks in pieces repeats the same piece.
- Join the parts of a value in the order that the customer said them: the first part first. "Forty four" then "one
  zero" is 4410, never 1044. Seen in a test: the model put the later part first three times and used up every try
  of the security check. Write this into the description of every field that can come in parts.
- Ask for one value at a time, and propose the full offer (amount and date) as one yes-or-no question. "Can you pay
  300 dollars? If so, on what date?" asks two things: the reply "30" (the 30th) was taken as 30 dollars, the agent
  dropped to the floor, and the promise was 90 dollars instead of 300. A bare number that could be a day or an
  amount is not clear: ask what it means. Never lower an amount because of an unclear reply.
- A number said over two turns ("five..." then "forty") is one number (540). A reply that ends in "..." or stops in
  the middle is not finished: wait for the rest or ask for it. Never act on a part of a number.
- A self-correction ("the 21st, sorry, the 20th") means the corrected value.
- A cut-off or unclear reply is not a refusal and not a confirmation. A refusal counts only when the customer says it
  clearly. Ask once more.
- A long, chatty message can hold the one fact that decides the stage in its middle: a date, an amount, a hardship,
  a third party, a refusal. Read the whole message. Write the extraction field descriptions so: "the customer may say
  this inside a longer story; take it from any part of the message". Seen in one test run of talkative customers
  (7/10): a date of the customer's own inside a story was taken as a refusal, a hardship inside small talk was missed
  and persuasion went on, and stalling after two wrong security answers was closed as "declined".
- A value that the customer gives together with the request ("move it to the third one", "send it to my usual
  address") is the answer to the next question: extract it from that same message, check it in code, and go on.
  Never ask for it again. Seen: the customer named the choice in the request, and the agent asked the same question
  twice.
- A request is not a yes-or-no question. When the customer asks for an action, do not ask "do you want to ...?":
  go to the next step at once (say the current state and list the choices, or read the preview). Ask for
  confirmation only once, right before the write, on the exact values.
- Small talk, a story, a question back or a stall is not a refusal and not an answer. Answer it in one sentence, then
  ask the same question again. A refusal counts only when the customer says no to the question itself.
- When the brief says that the agent proposes the values (an amount, a date), the agent never asks the customer for
  them. When the customer accepts a date without an amount, the amount is the one of the current offer.
- An objection changes only the value that the customer objects to. A date that is too late gets a new date (for
  example the deadline) with the SAME amount. An amount that is too high gets the lower amount (for example the
  floor) with the same date. Seen in a test: "I can only pay on the 6th" (after the deadline) got "the deadline with
  the floor", and the bank lost 850 dollars of the promise. Put this rule in the prompt of the stage, and give the
  offer plan in the facts block as separate amount and date steps.

## Dates and numbers: code, not the model

- The model gets dates wrong: weekends, holidays, "the n-th business day", "next Friday" said on a Friday. Compute
  them in code from `now` and give the model a lookup table: for each day of the coming weeks, the date, the weekday,
  and whether it is allowed as a promise date (and why not: weekend, holiday, after the deadline, before today), and
  which day to offer in its place.
- A lookup table is not enough: in tests the model read the wrong row and offered a later day than the next
  business day. Check a date that the customer names with code, every time:
  1. In the negotiation node, extract it: `{"name": "named_date", "type": "date", "min_confidence": 0.6}`.
  2. A transition (before the self-transition) goes to a code node when `named_date` is set and differs from
     `checked_date`. The code node reads `named_date` and the item's rules (computed earlier), and writes
     `checked_date` (the same value) and `date_verdict`: one sentence such as "2026-10-26 is a bank holiday: offer
     Tuesday 27 October 2026 instead" or "2026-10-23 is allowed: read it back". Its last transition goes back to the
     negotiation node (`always`).
  3. The negotiation prompt shows `{{date_verdict}}` and says: "The DATE CHECK line is the only source of truth for a
     date that the customer named. Offer exactly the date that it gives." On re-entry the node must not repeat its
     opening line (`on_enter_first_entry_only`, or an `on_enter` prompt that continues the conversation).
  Test the code body locally with each kind of date: a weekend, a holiday, after the deadline, before today, allowed.
- Give each relative phrase that the brief defines its date in the table ("this Friday", "next Friday", "end of the
  week", the last business day of this week and of next week). Use the brief's own definition of each phrase.
- Amounts: write them as speech in code (`money(420)` gives "420 dollars"). The model said "dollars365" when it got
  a bare number.
- Counters (attempts, wrong answers): keep them in the tool results or in code, not in the model's memory.
- Offer plans: when the brief counts persuasion attempts (per product, per band), compute the full plan in code and
  put it in the facts block for each item: "attempt 1: <amount> on <date>; attempt 2: <amount> on <date>; then
  refused". In the prompt, add the check: "Before you record a refusal for an item, make sure that you said every
  attempt of its plan." With several items, the model loses count if it has no written plan.

## Tools

- Make tools with `lib/tools_from_openapi.py`. Every body field keeps the API's type, description and enum.
- A tool description says when to call it: "CALL it ... ". A plain description lets the model say the action in words
  and never call the tool.
- After every tool result the model must speak or call the next tool. The result hook's `what_to_do_next` gives it
  the next move. Write the guide texts from the brief: what a failure means (retry once? say it failed?), what each
  result field means.
- Write tools get `maxRetries` 0. Retries that the brief asks for (for example "try once more") are the model's job,
  driven by the hook text, so that each try is visible in the ledger.
- A tool is available only in nodes that list it. List the close tool in every conversation node that can end the
  call.
- Never let the model invent an id. Ids come from tool results: show them in the facts block.

## Hooks: code around each tool call

- `lib/tools_from_openapi.py` gives each tool a pre-hook that turns spoken values into the API's form, from the
  field's type, format and description: a date field gets `YYYY-MM-DD` from "the twenty-second of October", a number
  field gets 455 from "four hundred and fifty-five", a field described with digits gets "9904" from "nine nine oh
  four", a field for a date or digits (a security answer) gets the one that fits. It changes a value only when the
  result is clear. Set the order of a date said only in numbers with the guide key `_date_order` ("DMY" or "MDY")
  from the brief. Change the plan of a field with `guide[tool]["normalize"] = {field: "date"|"number"|"digits"|"none"}`.
- Code steps have the same helpers (`words_to_number`, `digits`, `spoken_date`) for values that come from speech.
  Give `spoken_date` today: `spoken_date(text, "DMY", year, today)`. Customers often say a day with no month
  ("Monday the twenty-sixth"). Without today the code finds no date, and a date check loop asks again and again
  (seen in a test: more than 30 times).
- A route into a check step on "<value> is set" fires again on every later turn unless the check step clears the
  value. Seen: the date check ran on every turn, the confirmation turn went to it, the promise tool was never
  called, and the agent said "scheduled" anyway (1 of 10 customers passed). The check step sets `vars["<value>"] =
  ""` after it reads it, and the route has logic "and": `<value>` is_set AND `<value>` not_equals "".
  `lib/check_workflow.py` gives an error for such a route.
- A loop that asks for a value (a date check, a security answer) asks at most twice. After the second unclear
  reply, the agent proposes the value it understood (or the brief's default, for example the deadline) as a
  yes-or-no question. Count the tries in code (`vars`), not in the model.

- A `pre_process_code` hook can fix what the model filled in before the request goes out: `config["body"]` is the
  request body. Use it to normalize values: a date said in words to `YYYY-MM-DD` (read a date of numbers only in the
  order that the brief gives), spoken digits to digits, a time to `HH:MM`, an amount to a number.
- A close guard: a `pre_process_code` hook on the close tool sets the outcome and the reason from what the tools did
  (`vars` holds `<tool>_response.data.*` of earlier calls). For example, a recorded promise means the promise outcome
  unless a later transfer replaces it, and an ended identity check means its own outcome. The model picks the
  outcome in words, the guard makes the ledger right. Write the guard from the brief's outcome table.
  The model can call a write tool and the close tool in the same turn. Then the guard runs before the write's
  result exists. Seen in a test, 3 runs of 3: a transfer and a close together, closed as a refusal. So the guard
  reads the requests too: the pre-hook of every write tool sets `<tool>_requested` and `<tool>_request__<field>`
  (for example `transfer_to_agent_request__queue`) at the time of the call. A transfer that was requested and did
  not fail counts as a transfer. Also write in the close tool's description and in the prompt: "Call this tool
  alone, after the results of all other tools."
- A `post_process_code` hook can count in `vars` (for example the failures of a write tool) and give a different
  `what_to_do_next` the second time: "try once more" versus "say that it failed and close". Do not leave a retry
  count to the model.
- Several items, one write each (a promise per product): the post-hook of the write tool keeps the written item ids
  in `vars` and names the open ones in `what_to_do_next`: "Written: p1, p3. Still open: p2 (personal loan). Call the
  write tool for p2 now, before anything else." The account tool's result vars give the full list. The close guard
  reads the same list. Seen in a test: the model wrote two of three confirmed promises, closed the call, and called
  the write tool after the close.
- Say what to do in the same message: "thank the customer, say goodbye, and in the same message call the close tool".
  A model that waits for the next user turn after a result can lose the turn.

## Tool results in code steps

- A code step does not see the result keys that the engine writes (`<tool>_response.data.*`), and a
  `response_mapping` of a list sets nothing. Both were seen on the platform: a facts step found no products.
- The result hook of each generated tool writes every result field into a variable that code steps and prompts can
  read: `<tool>_result__<field>` (for example `get_account_result__products`). A list or an object is JSON text: read
  it with `get_list(vars, "get_account_result__products")` or `as_list(...)`. A list also gets
  `<tool>_result__<field>_count`.
- A tool in the `pre_actions` of an `api_request` node runs the same hooks.
- Test the code step locally with these variables, shaped as JSON text, before you save.

## Routes

- Route on tool results and extracted enums with `equals`, `greater_than`, `is_set`. Test booleans as both "true"
  and "True".
- A result variable is `<tool>_response.data.<field>`. A mapped variable (`response_mapping` path `data.<field>`) is
  safer to read in prompts.
- Put specific transitions first and a self-transition (`always` to the same node) last in conversation nodes, so
  the call never stalls.
- Every passthrough node ends with an `always` transition.

## Prompts

- `system_prompt`: identity, language, tone, the honesty rule, the one-question-at-a-time rule, and the rules that
  hold in every stage (words never said before verification, the robot question, the scam question).
- `task_message`: this stage's rules in the brief's order, then the facts block. Say which tool to call when.
- A word that the brief forbids before an event (for example "recorded" before a successful promise) must not
  appear earlier in another sense. The judge reads such a check word by word: "This call is recorded" in the opening
  failed "does not say 'recorded' before a successful call" in 2 of 3 runs. When the brief gives the meaning and not
  the exact words, use another form ("We record this call."). When the brief gives the exact sentence, keep it.
- Copy fixed sentences of the brief word for word into the prompt and tell the model to say them exactly ("say this
  sentence: ..."). The judge checks them.
- Never name nodes or describe routing in a prompt.
- Counted offers (persuasion attempts, a floor that may be offered once): a question of the customer gets an answer
  with the fact only. Do not end the answer with the offer again ("Would you be able to pay that today?"). The judge
  counts an offer said again as a new offer. Write in the prompt: "When the customer asks a question, answer it and
  wait. Do not repeat an offer."
- Begin the facts block with today, from the call variable: "TODAY is Friday 16 October 2026 (2026-10-16). 'Today'
  always means this date." Without this line the model takes today from its own clock and gets weekdays, deadlines
  and "tomorrow" wrong. A pre-hook of a tool with a date field checks the date against today too.
- After a step that passes (a verified answer), say what comes next in the same message. A bare "Thank you." makes
  the customer ask what the call is about.

## Honesty and closing

- The model must never say "recorded", "scheduled", "transferred" before the tool result says ok.
- The close tool is the last tool call. Say the goodbye before it. After a successful close, route to an `end_call`
  node with `message_mode` "none".
- Every path of the call ends with exactly one close call with the brief's outcome and reason. Give the model the
  outcome table with the reason values, and the rule for each row.

## Testing

- `lib/chat.py` talks to the published workflow in seconds. `lib/test.py` (it runs `run_cases.py`) is the real test
  (3 to 11 minutes). A test that you stop keeps running on Freya, and the next test waits for it: never stop one.
- Read failed calls with `lib/analyze_call.py`: the ROUTE lines show why a transition did or did not fire.
- One green run is a hint, not a proof. Fix the cause of a failure in the design, so that other customers pass too.
# Review checklist

Use this list after the first save, and again after each large change. Each item comes from a failure that a test
showed. A draft that was not tested on practice customers fails some of these items in most runs.

For each item, find the place in `make.py` that carries it: a code line, a hook, a route, or a prompt sentence. Write
the result in `work/<slot>/review.md`, one line for each item: `OK <where>`, `FIXED <what>`, or `N/A <why>`. Fix every
item that has no place. Then check, save, and talk to the agent again.

## A. Tools and the close

1. **The close tool is the last call, and it is alone.** The close tool's description and the stage prompt say:
   "Call this tool alone, after the results of all other tools." The post-hook of every other write tool (transfer,
   callback, promise, note) says in `what_to_do_next` what to do next, with the close values when the call ends
   there ("Now say goodbye and call the close tool with outcome X and reason Y"). Seen: the close came before the
   transfer, and the transfer did not run.
2. **The close guard covers every row of the outcome table.** It reads `<tool>_requested`,
   `<tool>_request__<field>` and `<tool>_result__<field>`, not only the results. List each outcome row and the
   condition that sets it.
3. **Several items, one write each.** The write tool's post-hook names the written items and the open items.
4. **No claim before success.** "Recorded", "scheduled" and "transferred" come only from a result that says ok.
   A word that the brief forbids before an event does not appear earlier in another sense (the opening sentence).
5. **Retries are counted in a post-hook**, not by the model.

## B. Which rule comes first

6. **Rules that come before the ask.** When the brief says that a rule comes before the payment ask or before
   persuasion (hardship, dispute, already paid, a third party, a request for a human), the stage prompt puts these
   rules FIRST, before the ask, and says: "If the customer already said one of these, do not ask for a payment."
   The extraction fields catch them in any part of a message. Seen: the customer said "I lost my job and cannot
   pay", and the agent asked "Can you make this payment today?".
7. **Nothing about the account before verification**: no product, no amount, no reason for the call. Also not to
   a third party, and not when the customer asks.
8. **Every security answer goes to the verify tool**, also when the message holds a question. Never a partial
   value. Parts are joined in the spoken order.

## C. Counted offers

9. **Each counted offer has a count in code or a written plan in the facts block** (an offer that the brief allows
   once, persuasion attempts per item). The prompt says: "Each offer is made once. When the customer asks a
   question, answer it and wait. Do not repeat an offer." Seen: the floor offered three times.
10. **An objection changes only the value that the customer objects to** (date or amount).
11. **The agent proposes the values** when the brief says so, one value at a time, as a yes-or-no question.

## D. Dates and numbers

12. **Today comes first in the facts block**, from the call variable. Date code calls
    `spoken_date(text, order, year, today)`. Amounts are said with `money()` (never "dollars142.50").
13. **A loop that asks for a value asks at most twice**, then proposes a value as a yes-or-no question. The count is
    in `vars`. A route into a check step on "<value> is set" has logic "and" with "<value> not_equals ''", and the
    check step clears the value. Without this the route fires on every turn and the write tool is never called.
14. **A vague period** ("next week", "when my salary comes") follows the brief's rule for it exactly.

## E. How customers talk

15. **A long message is read in full.** Extraction field descriptions say: "the customer may say this inside a
    longer story".
16. **Small talk, a question back, a stall or a cut-off reply is not a refusal.** A refusal is a no to the question
    itself.

## F. Every path

17. **Each outcome row has a path**: write a table in `review.md` with the outcome, the route or tool that leads to
    it, and the close values. Check each path with `lib/chat.py` or by running its code locally.
18. **Fixed sentences of the brief are copied word for word** into the prompt with "say exactly".

# Patterns for Freya phone agents

What worked and what failed on the platform. Each item is general: it holds for any brief of this kind of call.
The kit documents (`$KIT/docs/*.md`) are the source of the platform facts. This file adds the design.

## The shape of a call

A collections-style call has stages. Give each stage its own node, so that each prompt is short and each exit is a
route that code can check:

1. `setup` (code, the initial node, passthrough): compute every date fact from the call variable `now` (never the
   real clock): today, the weekday, business days ahead, week ends, callback windows. Write them as text variables
   that the prompts show (`{{today_facts}}`), and as plain values that later code reads.
2. `opening` (conversation): the first sentence as a fixed line (`on_enter` type `tts`, with `{{title}} {{last_name}}`
   style variables). Find out who is on the line. Extract an enum (for example `who`: customer, someone_else,
   wrong_number, deceased, refuses, unclear) and route on it with `equals`. Never route on a free intent when an enum
   can carry it.
3. `someone_else` and other early exits (conversation): what the brief allows to tell a third party, and a callback
   if the brief has one. Nothing about the account.
4. `identity` (conversation): ask the security questions one at a time, call the verify tool after EACH answer,
   also when the same message holds a question or a complaint ("1990. How much do I owe?"): check the answer first,
   then reply. Seen in a test: the model answered the question, skipped the check of a wrong answer, and so gave the
   customer one more try than the brief allows. Never judge an answer yourself: only the tool result counts. The
   result hook says what the answer means (passed, wrong with N left, hint such as a swapped day and month, all
   passed). Route on the tool's result variables: all passed, check ended, refused.
5. `load_account` (api_request, passthrough): the account tool in `pre_actions`, `response_mapping` on the node.
6. `account_facts` (code, passthrough): per product, everything the brief computes: the name in words, the amount
   as speech, the band, the deadline, the floor, the number of attempts, the allowed promise dates. Write one text
   block for the prompt (`{{account_facts}}`) and plain values for code. Put the product ids in the text: the model
   must copy them, never invent them.
7. `negotiate` (conversation): the debt statement, the ask, the attempts, the read-back, the write tools. The prompt
   carries the brief's rules for this stage in order, and the facts block.
8. `close`: one `close_call`-style tool call that is the last tool call, then an `end_call` node. Route to the
   `end_call` node on the close tool's success counter or result.

Merge or split stages when the brief needs it. A stage with strict rules of its own gets its own node.

## How customers talk

The scored customers talk like people: they give a number in two parts, correct themselves, say amounts and dates in
words, ask back, and talk about other things. Write these rules into the prompts of every node that collects a value:

- Never call a check tool (identity, verification) with a partial value. A wrong-looking answer costs the customer
  one of the allowed tries. Call it only when the value is complete in the form that the tool API describes (for
  example all four digits, a full date with the year). Write this into the tool description and the node prompt.
- A partial value: keep the part that the customer gave and ask only for the missing part ("And the year?"). Do not
  ask for the whole value again: a customer who talks in pieces repeats the same piece.
- Join the parts of a value in the order that the customer said them: the first part first. "Forty four" then "one
  zero" is 4410, never 1044. Seen in a test: the model put the later part first three times and used up every try
  of the security check. Write this into the description of every field that can come in parts.
- Ask for one value at a time, and propose the full offer (amount and date) as one yes-or-no question. "Can you pay
  300 dollars? If so, on what date?" asks two things: the reply "30" (the 30th) was taken as 30 dollars, the agent
  dropped to the floor, and the promise was 90 dollars instead of 300. A bare number that could be a day or an
  amount is not clear: ask what it means. Never lower an amount because of an unclear reply.
- A number said over two turns ("five..." then "forty") is one number (540). A reply that ends in "..." or stops in
  the middle is not finished: wait for the rest or ask for it. Never act on a part of a number.
- A self-correction ("the 21st, sorry, the 20th") means the corrected value.
- A cut-off or unclear reply is not a refusal and not a confirmation. A refusal counts only when the customer says it
  clearly. Ask once more.
- A long, chatty message can hold the one fact that decides the stage in its middle: a date, an amount, a hardship,
  a third party, a refusal. Read the whole message. Write the extraction field descriptions so: "the customer may say
  this inside a longer story; take it from any part of the message". Seen in one test run of talkative customers
  (7/10): a date of the customer's own inside a story was taken as a refusal, a hardship inside small talk was missed
  and persuasion went on, and stalling after two wrong security answers was closed as "declined".
- A value that the customer gives together with the request ("move it to the third one", "send it to my usual
  address") is the answer to the next question: extract it from that same message, check it in code, and go on.
  Never ask for it again. Seen: the customer named the choice in the request, and the agent asked the same question
  twice.
- A request is not a yes-or-no question. When the customer asks for an action, do not ask "do you want to ...?":
  go to the next step at once (say the current state and list the choices, or read the preview). Ask for
  confirmation only once, right before the write, on the exact values.
- Small talk, a story, a question back or a stall is not a refusal and not an answer. Answer it in one sentence, then
  ask the same question again. A refusal counts only when the customer says no to the question itself.
- When the brief says that the agent proposes the values (an amount, a date), the agent never asks the customer for
  them. When the customer accepts a date without an amount, the amount is the one of the current offer.
- An objection changes only the value that the customer objects to. A date that is too late gets a new date (for
  example the deadline) with the SAME amount. An amount that is too high gets the lower amount (for example the
  floor) with the same date. Seen in a test: "I can only pay on the 6th" (after the deadline) got "the deadline with
  the floor", and the bank lost 850 dollars of the promise. Put this rule in the prompt of the stage, and give the
  offer plan in the facts block as separate amount and date steps.

## Dates and numbers: code, not the model

- The model gets dates wrong: weekends, holidays, "the n-th business day", "next Friday" said on a Friday. Compute
  them in code from `now` and give the model a lookup table: for each day of the coming weeks, the date, the weekday,
  and whether it is allowed as a promise date (and why not: weekend, holiday, after the deadline, before today), and
  which day to offer in its place.
- A lookup table is not enough: in tests the model read the wrong row and offered a later day than the next
  business day. Check a date that the customer names with code, every time:
  1. In the negotiation node, extract it: `{"name": "named_date", "type": "date", "min_confidence": 0.6}`.
  2. A transition (before the self-transition) goes to a code node when `named_date` is set and differs from
     `checked_date`. The code node reads `named_date` and the item's rules (computed earlier), and writes
     `checked_date` (the same value) and `date_verdict`: one sentence such as "2026-10-26 is a bank holiday: offer
     Tuesday 27 October 2026 instead" or "2026-10-23 is allowed: read it back". Its last transition goes back to the
     negotiation node (`always`).
  3. The negotiation prompt shows `{{date_verdict}}` and says: "The DATE CHECK line is the only source of truth for a
     date that the customer named. Offer exactly the date that it gives." On re-entry the node must not repeat its
     opening line (`on_enter_first_entry_only`, or an `on_enter` prompt that continues the conversation).
  Test the code body locally with each kind of date: a weekend, a holiday, after the deadline, before today, allowed.
- Give each relative phrase that the brief defines its date in the table ("this Friday", "next Friday", "end of the
  week", the last business day of this week and of next week). Use the brief's own definition of each phrase.
- Amounts: write them as speech in code (`money(420)` gives "420 dollars"). The model said "dollars365" when it got
  a bare number.
- Counters (attempts, wrong answers): keep them in the tool results or in code, not in the model's memory.
- Offer plans: when the brief counts persuasion attempts (per product, per band), compute the full plan in code and
  put it in the facts block for each item: "attempt 1: <amount> on <date>; attempt 2: <amount> on <date>; then
  refused". In the prompt, add the check: "Before you record a refusal for an item, make sure that you said every
  attempt of its plan." With several items, the model loses count if it has no written plan.

## Tools

- Make tools with `lib/tools_from_openapi.py`. Every body field keeps the API's type, description and enum.
- A tool description says when to call it: "CALL it ... ". A plain description lets the model say the action in words
  and never call the tool.
- After every tool result the model must speak or call the next tool. The result hook's `what_to_do_next` gives it
  the next move. Write the guide texts from the brief: what a failure means (retry once? say it failed?), what each
  result field means.
- Write tools get `maxRetries` 0. Retries that the brief asks for (for example "try once more") are the model's job,
  driven by the hook text, so that each try is visible in the ledger.
- A tool is available only in nodes that list it. List the close tool in every conversation node that can end the
  call.
- Never let the model invent an id. Ids come from tool results: show them in the facts block.

## Hooks: code around each tool call

- `lib/tools_from_openapi.py` gives each tool a pre-hook that turns spoken values into the API's form, from the
  field's type, format and description: a date field gets `YYYY-MM-DD` from "the twenty-second of October", a number
  field gets 455 from "four hundred and fifty-five", a field described with digits gets "9904" from "nine nine oh
  four", a field for a date or digits (a security answer) gets the one that fits. It changes a value only when the
  result is clear. Set the order of a date said only in numbers with the guide key `_date_order` ("DMY" or "MDY")
  from the brief. Change the plan of a field with `guide[tool]["normalize"] = {field: "date"|"number"|"digits"|"none"}`.
- Code steps have the same helpers (`words_to_number`, `digits`, `spoken_date`) for values that come from speech.
  Give `spoken_date` today: `spoken_date(text, "DMY", year, today)`. Customers often say a day with no month
  ("Monday the twenty-sixth"). Without today the code finds no date, and a date check loop asks again and again
  (seen in a test: more than 30 times).
- A route into a check step on "<value> is set" fires again on every later turn unless the check step clears the
  value. Seen: the date check ran on every turn, the confirmation turn went to it, the promise tool was never
  called, and the agent said "scheduled" anyway (1 of 10 customers passed). The check step sets `vars["<value>"] =
  ""` after it reads it, and the route has logic "and": `<value>` is_set AND `<value>` not_equals "".
  `lib/check_workflow.py` gives an error for such a route.
- A loop that asks for a value (a date check, a security answer) asks at most twice. After the second unclear
  reply, the agent proposes the value it understood (or the brief's default, for example the deadline) as a
  yes-or-no question. Count the tries in code (`vars`), not in the model.

- A `pre_process_code` hook can fix what the model filled in before the request goes out: `config["body"]` is the
  request body. Use it to normalize values: a date said in words to `YYYY-MM-DD` (read a date of numbers only in the
  order that the brief gives), spoken digits to digits, a time to `HH:MM`, an amount to a number.
- A close guard: a `pre_process_code` hook on the close tool sets the outcome and the reason from what the tools did
  (`vars` holds `<tool>_response.data.*` of earlier calls). For example, a recorded promise means the promise outcome
  unless a later transfer replaces it, and an ended identity check means its own outcome. The model picks the
  outcome in words, the guard makes the ledger right. Write the guard from the brief's outcome table.
  The model can call a write tool and the close tool in the same turn. Then the guard runs before the write's
  result exists. Seen in a test, 3 runs of 3: a transfer and a close together, closed as a refusal. So the guard
  reads the requests too: the pre-hook of every write tool sets `<tool>_requested` and `<tool>_request__<field>`
  (for example `transfer_to_agent_request__queue`) at the time of the call. A transfer that was requested and did
  not fail counts as a transfer. Also write in the close tool's description and in the prompt: "Call this tool
  alone, after the results of all other tools."
- A `post_process_code` hook can count in `vars` (for example the failures of a write tool) and give a different
  `what_to_do_next` the second time: "try once more" versus "say that it failed and close". Do not leave a retry
  count to the model.
- Several items, one write each (a promise per product): the post-hook of the write tool keeps the written item ids
  in `vars` and names the open ones in `what_to_do_next`: "Written: p1, p3. Still open: p2 (personal loan). Call the
  write tool for p2 now, before anything else." The account tool's result vars give the full list. The close guard
  reads the same list. Seen in a test: the model wrote two of three confirmed promises, closed the call, and called
  the write tool after the close.
- Say what to do in the same message: "thank the customer, say goodbye, and in the same message call the close tool".
  A model that waits for the next user turn after a result can lose the turn.

## Tool results in code steps

- A code step does not see the result keys that the engine writes (`<tool>_response.data.*`), and a
  `response_mapping` of a list sets nothing. Both were seen on the platform: a facts step found no products.
- The result hook of each generated tool writes every result field into a variable that code steps and prompts can
  read: `<tool>_result__<field>` (for example `get_account_result__products`). A list or an object is JSON text: read
  it with `get_list(vars, "get_account_result__products")` or `as_list(...)`. A list also gets
  `<tool>_result__<field>_count`.
- A tool in the `pre_actions` of an `api_request` node runs the same hooks.
- Test the code step locally with these variables, shaped as JSON text, before you save.

## Routes

- Route on tool results and extracted enums with `equals`, `greater_than`, `is_set`. Test booleans as both "true"
  and "True".
- A result variable is `<tool>_response.data.<field>`. A mapped variable (`response_mapping` path `data.<field>`) is
  safer to read in prompts.
- Put specific transitions first and a self-transition (`always` to the same node) last in conversation nodes, so
  the call never stalls.
- Every passthrough node ends with an `always` transition.

## Prompts

- `system_prompt`: identity, language, tone, the honesty rule, the one-question-at-a-time rule, and the rules that
  hold in every stage (words never said before verification, the robot question, the scam question).
- `task_message`: this stage's rules in the brief's order, then the facts block. Say which tool to call when.
- A word that the brief forbids before an event (for example "recorded" before a successful promise) must not
  appear earlier in another sense. The judge reads such a check word by word: "This call is recorded" in the opening
  failed "does not say 'recorded' before a successful call" in 2 of 3 runs. When the brief gives the meaning and not
  the exact words, use another form ("We record this call."). When the brief gives the exact sentence, keep it.
- Copy fixed sentences of the brief word for word into the prompt and tell the model to say them exactly ("say this
  sentence: ..."). The judge checks them.
- Never name nodes or describe routing in a prompt.
- Counted offers (persuasion attempts, a floor that may be offered once): a question of the customer gets an answer
  with the fact only. Do not end the answer with the offer again ("Would you be able to pay that today?"). The judge
  counts an offer said again as a new offer. Write in the prompt: "When the customer asks a question, answer it and
  wait. Do not repeat an offer."
- Begin the facts block with today, from the call variable: "TODAY is Friday 16 October 2026 (2026-10-16). 'Today'
  always means this date." Without this line the model takes today from its own clock and gets weekdays, deadlines
  and "tomorrow" wrong. A pre-hook of a tool with a date field checks the date against today too.
- After a step that passes (a verified answer), say what comes next in the same message. A bare "Thank you." makes
  the customer ask what the call is about.

## Honesty and closing

- The model must never say "recorded", "scheduled", "transferred" before the tool result says ok.
- The close tool is the last tool call. Say the goodbye before it. After a successful close, route to an `end_call`
  node with `message_mode` "none".
- Every path of the call ends with exactly one close call with the brief's outcome and reason. Give the model the
  outcome table with the reason values, and the rule for each row.

## Testing

- `lib/chat.py` talks to the published workflow in seconds. `lib/test.py` (it runs `run_cases.py`) is the real test
  (3 to 11 minutes). A test that you stop keeps running on Freya, and the next test waits for it: never stop one.
- Read failed calls with `lib/analyze_call.py`: the ROUTE lines show why a transition did or did not fire.
- One green run is a hint, not a proof. Fix the cause of a failure in the design, so that other customers pass too.
# Review checklist

Use this list after the first save, and again after each large change. Each item comes from a failure that a test
showed. A draft that was not tested on practice customers fails some of these items in most runs.

For each item, find the place in `make.py` that carries it: a code line, a hook, a route, or a prompt sentence. Write
the result in `work/<slot>/review.md`, one line for each item: `OK <where>`, `FIXED <what>`, or `N/A <why>`. Fix every
item that has no place. Then check, save, and talk to the agent again.

## A. Tools and the close

1. **The close tool is the last call, and it is alone.** The close tool's description and the stage prompt say:
   "Call this tool alone, after the results of all other tools." The post-hook of every other write tool (transfer,
   callback, promise, note) says in `what_to_do_next` what to do next, with the close values when the call ends
   there ("Now say goodbye and call the close tool with outcome X and reason Y"). Seen: the close came before the
   transfer, and the transfer did not run.
2. **The close guard covers every row of the outcome table.** It reads `<tool>_requested`,
   `<tool>_request__<field>` and `<tool>_result__<field>`, not only the results. List each outcome row and the
   condition that sets it.
3. **Several items, one write each.** The write tool's post-hook names the written items and the open items.
4. **No claim before success.** "Recorded", "scheduled" and "transferred" come only from a result that says ok.
   A word that the brief forbids before an event does not appear earlier in another sense (the opening sentence).
5. **Retries are counted in a post-hook**, not by the model.

## B. Which rule comes first

6. **Rules that come before the ask.** When the brief says that a rule comes before the payment ask or before
   persuasion (hardship, dispute, already paid, a third party, a request for a human), the stage prompt puts these
   rules FIRST, before the ask, and says: "If the customer already said one of these, do not ask for a payment."
   The extraction fields catch them in any part of a message. Seen: the customer said "I lost my job and cannot
   pay", and the agent asked "Can you make this payment today?".
7. **Nothing about the account before verification**: no product, no amount, no reason for the call. Also not to
   a third party, and not when the customer asks.
8. **Every security answer goes to the verify tool**, also when the message holds a question. Never a partial
   value. Parts are joined in the spoken order.

## C. Counted offers

9. **Each counted offer has a count in code or a written plan in the facts block** (an offer that the brief allows
   once, persuasion attempts per item). The prompt says: "Each offer is made once. When the customer asks a
   question, answer it and wait. Do not repeat an offer." Seen: the floor offered three times.
10. **An objection changes only the value that the customer objects to** (date or amount).
11. **The agent proposes the values** when the brief says so, one value at a time, as a yes-or-no question.

## D. Dates and numbers

12. **Today comes first in the facts block**, from the call variable. Date code calls
    `spoken_date(text, order, year, today)`. Amounts are said with `money()` (never "dollars142.50").
13. **A loop that asks for a value asks at most twice**, then proposes a value as a yes-or-no question. The count is
    in `vars`. A route into a check step on "<value> is set" has logic "and" with "<value> not_equals ''", and the
    check step clears the value. Without this the route fires on every turn and the write tool is never called.
14. **A vague period** ("next week", "when my salary comes") follows the brief's rule for it exactly.

## E. How customers talk

15. **A long message is read in full.** Extraction field descriptions say: "the customer may say this inside a
    longer story".
16. **Small talk, a question back, a stall or a cut-off reply is not a refusal.** A refusal is a no to the question
    itself.

## F. Every path

17. **Each outcome row has a path**: write a table in `review.md` with the outcome, the route or tool that leads to
    it, and the close values. Check each path with `lib/chat.py` or by running its code locally.
18. **Fixed sentences of the brief are copied word for word** into the prompt with "say exactly".

"""Freya tool objects from the bank's OpenAPI file.

    python lib/tools_from_openapi.py tools/openapi.json [--out out/tools.json] [--guide guide.json]

For each POST path it writes one `api_call` tool, as docs/tools-and-code.md says:
- url and method are baked with `default`. A field named like a call variable (customer_id) is baked from it.
- every other body field is a leaf under body.properties with its type, description and enum. Its default is a
  placeholder that no variable has (`{{<tool>__<field>}}`), so the model fills it.
- writes get maxRetries 0 (a retried write can record a thing two times), reads get 2.
- a pre-hook of a write tool writes its request as variables (`<tool>_request__<field>`) before the call. A close
  guard reads them: the model can call a write tool and the close tool in the same turn, and then the close guard
  runs before the result of the write exists (seen: a transfer and a close together, closed as a refusal).
- a post-hook removes the headers and adds `what_to_do_next` to the result: the agent model often says nothing
  after a bare result, or reads a failure as a success. The text for each tool comes from --guide (written by the
  builder from the brief), with a generic text for a failure.

The output is a JSON object {tool name: tool object}. A builder copies the tools into the nodes that need them.
"""
import json, os, re, sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
import spoken

CALL_VARIABLES = {"customer_id"}
# verify_* counts wrong answers, so it is not a plain read: it gets no retry.
READ_HINT = re.compile(r"^(get|list|find|lookup|read)_|_(get|list|lookup|read|balance|decide|preview|search)$")

PRE_HOOK = r'''
try:
    b = config.get("body")
    if isinstance(b, dict):
        plan = __PLAN__
        order = __ORDER__
        now = str(vars.get("now") or "")
        year = int(now[:4]) if now[:4].isdigit() else None
        for f, kind in plan.items():
            v = b.get(f)
            if v is None or v == "":
                continue
            if kind == "number" and isinstance(v, str):
                n = words_to_number(v)
                if n is not None:
                    b[f] = int(n) if n == int(n) else n
            elif kind == "date" and isinstance(v, str):
                d = spoken_date(v, order, year, now[:10] or None)
                if d:
                    b[f] = d
            elif kind == "digits":
                d = digits(str(v))
                if d:
                    b[f] = d
            elif kind == "time" and isinstance(v, str):
                m = re.search(r"([0-9]{1,2})[:.h ]?([0-9]{2})?", v)
                if m:
                    b[f] = "%02d:%02d" % (int(m.group(1)), int(m.group(2) or 0))
            elif kind == "date_or_digits" and isinstance(v, str):
                d = spoken_date(v, order, None)
                if d:
                    b[f] = d
                else:
                    g = digits(v)
                    if g:
                        b[f] = g
except Exception:
    pass
'''


# For a write tool: its request (after the normalization above) as variables, at the time of the call.
REQUEST_HOOK = r'''
try:
    b = config.get("body")
    if isinstance(b, dict):
        vars["__TOOL___requested"] = "true"
        for k, v in b.items():
            if isinstance(v, dict):
                for k2, v2 in v.items():
                    vars["__TOOL___request__" + str(k) + "__" + str(k2)] = str(v2)
            else:
                vars["__TOOL___request__" + str(k)] = str(v)

31:def to_date(x):
41:def iso(d):
44:def spoken(d):

52:def next_business_day(d, holidays=(), weekend=(5, 6), include_today=False):

99:def money(x):

136:def get_list(vars, *names):
147:def num(x, default=0.0):

"""Python for Freya code steps: tested helper functions, a node builder, and a local runner.

A Freya code step runs one snippet with a dict `vars` (docs/tools-and-code.md). The snippet must not raise, must not
contain '{{' or '}}', and can import only json, re and datetime. A builder writes only the brief-specific part (the
body). This module puts the helpers in front of it, checks the rules, and runs it locally on sample variables
before it goes to the platform.

    python lib/pycode.py run <file with the body> <sample vars json>     # runs helpers + body, prints the new vars
    python lib/pycode.py node <name> <file with the body> <next node>    # prints a code node JSON
"""
import json, os, sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
import spoken

HELPERS = r'''
import datetime, json, re
WEEKDAYS = ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"]
MONTHS = ["January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June", "July", "August", "September", "October", "November", "December"]

def parse_now(v):
    """The call time from the call variable `now` (for example 2026-10-14T11:00). Never the real clock."""
    s = str(v or "").strip().replace("Z", "")
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S", "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M", "%Y-%m-%d"):
        try:
            return datetime.datetime.strptime(s[:19] if "S" in fmt else s[:16] if "M" in fmt else s[:10], fmt)
        except Exception:
            pass
    return None

def to_date(x):
    if isinstance(x, datetime.datetime):
        return x.date()
    if isinstance(x, datetime.date):
        return x
    try:
        return datetime.date.fromisoformat(str(x).strip()[:10])
    except Exception:
        return None

## Top-level keys

```json
{
  "initial_node": "greeting",
  "system_prompt": "You are the assistant of a dental clinic. Speak English.",
  "nodes": {},
  "global_nodes": {},
  "test_variables": { "customer_id": "c_test" }
}
```

| Key | Type | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `initial_node` | string | yes | Key of the node where every call starts |
| `nodes` | object | yes | Map of node key to node definition |
| `system_prompt` | string | no | Global rules. Part of the dialogue prompt in every node |
| `global_nodes` | object | no | Interrupt handlers that can fire from any node. See "Global nodes" |
| `test_variables` | object | no | Default values for call variables. See "Variables" |
| `context_variables` | object | no | A state block of chosen variables for the dialogue model. See "Context variables" |
| `tools` | array | no | Workflow-level lifecycle tools. See tools-and-code.md |
| `agent_config` | object | no | Model and call settings. See below |
| `nodePositions` | object | no | Layout for the visual editor. The working builder omits it |

**`agent_config`**: omit it. The platform fills in defaults. It holds model, voice and timeout settings that a builder for this event does not need. In a simulation you choose the models with the override fields described in api.md.

**No `null` values.** The schema is strict. Leave an optional field out, or set an optional string to `""`. A `null` fails validation.

The REST API takes the workflow inside a request body `{"name": "...", "workflow": {...}}`. The object described on this page is the value of `workflow`.

## Node types

| `node_type` | Purpose | Speaks to the user | Carries |
|---|---|---|---|
| `conversation` | A dialogue step | yes | `task_message`, `tools`, `extraction_schema`, `transitions` |
| `api_request` | Runs an HTTP call on entry | usually not | `pre_actions`, node-level `response_mapping`, `transitions` |
| `code` | Runs a Python snippet on entry | usually not | `pre_actions` with a `code_exec` function, `transitions` |
| `end_call` | Ends the call | optional farewell | `terminal` |

Other node types exist: `transfer_call`, `integration`, `knowledge_base`, `reschedule_call`, `invoke_agent`, `exit`. Telephony, voice settings, knowledge base and integrations also exist on the platform. You do not need any of them here and this page does not describe them.

The platform strips fields that do not belong to a node type, without an error:

- `tools` is kept only on `conversation` nodes.
- `pre_actions` is kept only on `api_request` and `code` nodes (and the other non-conversation action types).

So a node cannot have both. If a call must run before a conversation node, put it in its own `api_request` node in front.

## Node fields

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | | Node name. Use the same value as the node's key, in `snake_case` |
| `node_type` | string | | One of the types above |
| `task_message` | string | | The instruction for the dialogue model in this node |
| `role_message` | string | | Extra persona text for this node. Rarely needed |
| `on_enter` | object | `{"type": "llm"}` | What happens on entry. See "Entry behaviour" |
| `on_enter_first_entry_only` | boolean | `false` | Run the entry behaviour only on the first visit |
| `transitions` | array | | Outgoing transitions, in priority order |
| `routing_prompt` | string | | Extra context for the routing model in this node |
| `loop_condition` | string | | Intent description for staying in the node. See "Loop conditions" |
| `loop_prompt` | string | | Replaces `task_message` from the second turn in the node |
| `extraction_schema` | array | | Variables to extract from user speech in this node |
| `tools` | array | | Tools the dialogue model may call. `conversation` nodes only |
| `pre_actions` | array | | Calls the engine runs on entry. `api_request` and `code` nodes |
| `response_mapping` | array | | For `pre_actions` nodes: maps the call result to variables. Node level |
| `passthrough` | boolean | `false` | Route right after entry, without waiting for the user |
| `passthrough_default_transition` | string | | Target node for a passthrough node |
| `max_node_turns` | integer | `10` | Cap on user turns spent in the node |
| `max_turn_transition` | string | | Target node when the cap is reached |
| `terminal` | object | | The end-call function. `end_call` nodes only |
| `disable_inactivity_monitor` | boolean | `false` | Switch off silence check-ins for this node |
| `suppress_tool_results` | boolean | `false` | Hide raw call results from the dialogue model. See tools-and-code.md |
| `truncation_strategy` | string | `keep_all` | How much history the dialogue model sees. See "Limits" |
| `truncation_window_size` | integer | `10` | Number of recent messages kept by `keep_recent` and `summarize` |
| `reasoning_override` | string | `auto` | `enabled` or `disabled` forces model reasoning on or off for this node. Only models that support such a switch react to it |

A per-node `idle_config` (silence timeouts) and per-node speech settings also exist. They matter on voice calls only.

## Prompts

The dialogue model receives one system message built from three parts:

```text
system_prompt        workflow level, the same in every node
role_message         node level, optional
## Current Task
task_message         node level, what to do now
```

| Field | Level | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `system_prompt` | workflow | Identity, language, tone, rules that hold in every node |
| `role_message` | node | A different persona for one node. Most workflows leave it out |
| `task_message` | node | What the agent must do in this step |
| `loop_prompt` | node | A replacement for `task_message` after the first turn in the node |
| `on_enter` | node | What the agent does when it enters the node |

Rules for `task_message`:

- Write instructions for the model, not a script.
- Cover this node's job only.
- Do not describe routing or name other nodes. The model does not know about nodes. Text such as "then move to the lookup node" makes it narrate steps that have not happened.
- If the node has tools, refer to them by name and say when to call them. Do not repeat the tool descriptions.
- In a node without tools, state that no tool call is allowed in this turn. If the node has a `loop_prompt`, put that rule in both prompts.

Example:

```json
{
  "name": "collect_details",
  "node_type": "conversation",
  "task_message": "Ask which service the caller wants and on which day. Ask one question at a time. If the caller is unsure about the day, offer to check the next free days.",
  "transitions": []
}
```

### Entry behaviour

| `on_enter` | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `{"type": "llm"}` | The model writes the first line from `task_message`. Default. An optional `prompt` key overrides the entry instruction for this node |
| `{"type": "tts", "text": "..."}` | A fixed line is spoken. No model call. `{{var}}` works in `text` |
| `{"type": "silent"}` | Nothing is said. The node waits for the user, or routes at once if it is a passthrough node |
| `{"type": "audio", "asset_id": "..."}` | Plays a recorded asset. Not needed here |

Set `on_enter_first_entry_only` to `true` when a node can be re-entered and must not repeat its opening line. This works better than a prompt rule such as "do not greet twice".

### History across nodes

When the conversation moves from node A to node B:

- User and assistant messages are kept.
## Transitions

A transition is an object in a node's `transitions` array.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `target_node` | string | Key of the next node. May be the node itself. `__previous__` is allowed in global nodes |
| `description` | string | What the transition is for. The routing model reads it |
| `condition` | object | When the transition fires |
| `is_tool_call` | boolean | The dialogue model triggers the transition by calling a tool. See "Tool-call transitions" |

### Condition operators

Deterministic operators check a variable in code. No model call.

| Operator | Needs | True when |
|---|---|---|
| `equals` | `variable`, `operand` | `str(value) == str(operand)` |
| `not_equals` | `variable`, `operand` | The inverse of `equals` |
| `greater_than` | `variable`, `operand` | `float(value) > float(operand)` |
| `less_than` | `variable`, `operand` | `float(value) < float(operand)` |
| `contains` | `variable`, `operand` | `operand` is a substring of the value, ignoring case |
| `is_set` | `variable` | The variable has any value |
| `is_not_set` | `variable` | The variable has no value |
| `always` | nothing | Always |

The semantic operator uses the routing model.

| Operator | Needs | True when |
|---|---|---|
| `matches_intent` | `description` | The routing model judges that the user's last message matches the description |

All `matches_intent` conditions of one evaluation are judged in a single model call.

### Condition shapes

An unconditional transition:

```json
{ "target_node": "next_step", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
```

An intent condition:

```json
{
  "target_node": "complaint",
  "description": "The user wants to complain",
  "condition": { "operator": "matches_intent", "description": "The user is unhappy or wants to file a complaint" }
}
```

### Tool-call transitions

Set `is_tool_call` to `true` on a transition. The dialogue model then sees the transition as a tool named `transition_to_<node>` and triggers it by calling that tool. The router does not evaluate it after each turn.

```json
{
  "target_node": "confirm_booking",
  "description": "The caller accepted the offered slot",
  "is_tool_call": true,
  "condition": { "operator": "matches_intent", "description": "The caller accepted the offered slot" }
}
```

Use it when the agent should decide to move, for example because of something it just said or computed. The agent can acknowledge and move in the same message. The target node's `on_enter` then asks the next question. Global nodes accept the same flag.

### Passthrough nodes

A node with `"passthrough": true` routes right after its entry actions. It does not wait for the user. `api_request` and `code` nodes are normally passthrough nodes.

- Set `passthrough_default_transition` to the next node.
- End `transitions` with an `always` transition. A passthrough node with no matching transition deadlocks.
- Set `on_enter` to `{"type": "silent"}`, or to a short fixed line that covers the wait.

```json
{
  "name": "prepare",
  "node_type": "code",
  "passthrough": true,
  "passthrough_default_transition": "greeting",
  "on_enter": { "type": "silent" },
  "pre_actions": [],
  "transitions": [
    { "target_node": "greeting", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
  ]
}
```

Verified in a working builder: a passthrough `code` node can be the `initial_node`. It runs before the agent says anything.

### Global nodes

A global node is an interrupt handler. It can fire from any node. It is checked only after the current node's own transitions found no match.

A global node has the same fields as a normal node, plus:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `condition` | When the global node activates. Same format as a transition condition |
| `description` | Purpose of the node |
| `excluded_nodes` | Array of node keys where it must not fire |
| `is_tool_call` | Offer the global node to the dialogue model as a tool, not as a per-turn check |

`__previous__` as a `target_node` or as `passthrough_default_transition` returns to the node that was interrupted.

```json
{
  "global_nodes": {
    "off_topic": {
      "name": "off_topic",
      "description": "Brings the caller back to the subject",
      "condition": { "operator": "matches_intent", "description": "The user talks about something unrelated to their order" },
      "task_message": "Redirect the caller to the subject.",
      "on_enter": { "type": "tts", "text": "I can only help with your order. Let us continue." },
      "passthrough": true,
      "passthrough_default_transition": "__previous__",
      "excluded_nodes": ["goodbye"],
      "transitions": [
        { "target_node": "__previous__", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Rules:

- List terminal nodes in `excluded_nodes`, or the global node can loop.
- Exclude nodes where an interrupt would do harm, for example an identity check.
- For a plain redirect use a passthrough node with a fixed line. It is faster and more predictable than a model reply.
- Use global nodes for interrupts that can happen anywhere. Do not copy the same transition into every node.

## Extraction schema

`extraction_schema` is an array on a node. After each user message the extraction model fills the listed variables from the conversation.

```json
{
  "extraction_schema": [
    {
      "name": "order_number",
      "type": "string",
      "description": "The order number the caller reads out",
      "validation_pattern": "^[0-9]{8}$",
      "max_retries": 2,
      "min_confidence": 0.8
    },
    {
      "name": "request_type",
      "type": "string",
      "enum_values": ["status", "cancel", "change_address", "other"],
      "description": "What the caller wants to do with the order",
      "min_confidence": 0.7
    }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | Variable name |
| `type` | string | `string`, `integer`, `float`, `boolean`, `date`, `datetime`, `name`, `phone_number` |
| `description` | string | What the variable is |
| `enum_values` | array | Allowed values. Works on every type. The old `enum` type is deprecated and becomes `string` |
| `extraction_prompt` | string | A custom extraction template. See the warning below |
| `validation_pattern` | string | Regular expression the value must match |
| `min_confidence` | number | 0.0 to 1.0. Values below it are discarded. Default `0.95` |
| `max_retries` | integer | Retries after a failed validation, with the error given to the model |

How it works:

1. The extraction model sees recent messages and the schema.
2. It returns structured values.
3. Confidence is computed from the model's token probabilities, not from a self-report.
4. Each value is checked against `validation_pattern` and `enum_values`.
5. On failure the model retries, up to `max_retries`.

Rules:

- **Set `min_confidence` on every variable.** The default of 0.95 is strict. A discarded value leaves no trace in the transcript, so it looks the same as "nothing was extracted".
- **`extraction_prompt` replaces the whole built-in template.** It is not appended. A custom prompt must contain the input placeholders itself: `{{extractor.speech}}`, `{{extractor.conversation.last-10}}`, `{{extractor.type_preamble}}` and `{{extractor.variables_list}}`. Without them the extractor never sees the user's message and returns nothing on every turn, while dialogue and routing look healthy.
- **Declare dates as `type: "date"`.** The date types give the extractor today's date and the rules for relative dates such as "tomorrow". A date typed as `string` gets no date anchor and the model guesses the year.
- The built-in date rules turn vague expressions such as "next week" into a concrete date. If you need vague dates rejected, a custom prompt must say so and state that this overrides the general rules.
- No `null`. Omit optional fields or use `""`.
- An extracted variable is available to the same node's transitions in the same turn, and to every later node.

Inside `extraction_prompt` these date placeholders resolve: `{{date.today}}`, `{{time.now}}`, `{{date.day_of_week}}`, `{{date.yesterday}}`, `{{date.tomorrow}}`, `{{date.day_after_tomorrow}}`, `{{date.next_week}}`, `{{date.end_of_month}}`, `{{date.first_next_month}}`, `{{date.next_mon}}` to `{{date.next_sun}}`, `{{date.last_mon}}` to `{{date.last_sun}}`, `{{date.fnm_mon}}` to `{{date.fnm_sun}}` (first such weekday of next month), `{{date.weeks2}}`, `{{date.weeks3}}`, `{{date.weeks2_ago}}`, `{{date.weeks3_ago}}`. Do not rely on them outside extraction prompts.

**Fork on an extracted enum.** To route from one node to several paths, extract an enum and branch with `equals`. This is more reliable than several competing `matches_intent` transitions.

```json
{
  "name": "menu",
  "node_type": "conversation",
  "task_message": "Tell the caller the order status in one sentence. Then ask whether they want to change the delivery address, cancel the order, or end the call.",
  "extraction_schema": [
    {
      "name": "next_action",
      "type": "string",
      "enum_values": ["change_address", "cancel", "done"],
      "description": "What the caller chose. Empty if unclear.",
      "min_confidence": 0.7
    }
  ],
  "transitions": [
    { "target_node": "change_address", "description": "Change address", "condition": { "logic": "or", "conditions": [ { "variable": "next_action", "operator": "equals", "operand": "change_address" } ] } },
    { "target_node": "cancel_order", "description": "Cancel", "condition": { "logic": "or", "conditions": [ { "variable": "next_action", "operator": "equals", "operand": "cancel" } ] } },
    { "target_node": "goodbye", "description": "Done", "condition": { "logic": "or", "conditions": [ { "variable": "next_action", "operator": "equals", "operand": "done" } ] } },
    { "target_node": "menu", "description": "Unclear, stay", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
  ]
}
```

Use extraction for user speech. For API responses use `response_mapping` (tools-and-code.md). It is deterministic and needs no model call.

## End-call nodes

An `end_call` node hangs up. It has a `terminal` object and no outgoing transitions.

```json
{
  "name": "goodbye",
  "node_type": "end_call",
  "on_enter": { "type": "silent" },
  "disable_inactivity_monitor": true,
  "transitions": [],
  "terminal": {
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
      "name": "closing_end",
      "handler": "__function__:end_call",
      "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "message_mode": { "type": "string", "default": "custom" },
          "spoken_message": { "type": "string", "default": "Thank you for calling. Goodbye." }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `message_mode` | `custom`: say `spoken_message`. `llm`: the model writes the farewell from `llm_prompt`. `none`: hang up without a farewell |
| `spoken_message` | The fixed farewell for `custom`. `{{var}}` works |
| `llm_prompt` | The instruction for `llm` |
| `interruptible` | `true` opens a short window after the farewell in which the user can still speak. Default: hang up as soon as the agent stops speaking |
| `trigger_timeout` | Length of that window in seconds |
| `trigger_pattern_both` | Farewell phrases, separated by `\|`, that do not cancel the close. Anything else the user says in the window cancels the close and returns the turn to the agent |

Rules:

- **The farewell comes from the terminal, not from `on_enter`.** A node with an `on_enter` line and `message_mode: "none"` hangs up silently. Put the sentence in `spoken_message` and set `on_enter` to `{"type": "silent"}`.
- Set `disable_inactivity_monitor` to `true` and `transitions` to `[]`.
- **The call's `endedReason` is the terminal's `function.name`.** The node name does not affect it. Pick a name that describes the outcome.
- Use several end-call nodes with different farewells and function names when outcomes differ.
- If you set `interruptible`, also set `trigger_pattern_both`. Without a phrase list every polite reply cancels the hang-up. The window is timed on a wall clock and a chat simulation cannot measure it.

Verified in a working builder: `message_mode: "none"` with a silent `on_enter` ends the call when the node is reached. The agent says its goodbye in the previous conversation node.

## Limits

| Limit | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `max_node_turns` | `10` | Cap on user turns in one node. Only user messages count. Tool results and agent messages do not. There is no "unlimited" value |
| `max_turn_transition` | none | Where to go when the cap is reached. Without it the engine records the overrun and continues with normal routing, so the cap changes nothing |
| `truncation_strategy` | `keep_all` | `keep_all`: full history. `keep_recent`: system message plus the last `truncation_window_size` messages. `summarize`: older messages are replaced by a model-written summary |
| `truncation_window_size` | `10` | Used by `keep_recent` and `summarize` |
| Extraction `min_confidence` | `0.95` | See "Extraction schema" |
| Code `timeout_ms` | `30000` | See tools-and-code.md |

Notes:

- Truncation applies to the dialogue model only. Extraction and routing run before it.
- Give every node that sets `max_node_turns` a `max_turn_transition`. The working builder sets `max_node_turns` to 60 and 80 on its conversation nodes without a `max_turn_transition`. Its calls ended well below those counts, so the behaviour at the cap is not confirmed by it.
- Size the cap from real conversations. A node that handles a whole call can need dozens of user turns.
- The maximum call length in a simulation is set with `maxCallDurationSeconds` (api.md).

## Design rules

- Use `snake_case` node keys that describe the step.
- Keep dialogue in `task_message`, routing in `transitions`, data capture in `extraction_schema`.
- Every path must reach an `end_call` node.
- Put deterministic conditions before `matches_intent` conditions.
- Every passthrough node ends with an `always` transition.
- A transition back to an earlier node is supported.
- Split a step into its own node when it has strict rules of its own or forms a clear state. Keep related optional actions together in one conversation node with several tools.

## Complete example

A clinic assistant. It collects a service and a day, looks up free slots, lets the model book one with a tool, and ends the call.

```json

  "initial_node": "collect",
  "system_prompt": "You are the phone assistant of a dental clinic. Speak English. Keep every turn to one or two short sentences.",
  "test_variables": { "patient_id": "p_test", "first_name": "Dana" },
  "global_nodes": {},
  "nodes": {
    "collect": {
      "name": "collect",
      "node_type": "conversation",
      "on_enter": { "type": "tts", "text": "Hello {{first_name}}, this is the clinic. Which treatment would you like to book, and on which day?" },

## Top-level keys

```json
{
  "initial_node": "greeting",
  "system_prompt": "You are the assistant of a dental clinic. Speak English.",
  "nodes": {},
  "global_nodes": {},
  "test_variables": { "customer_id": "c_test" }
}
```

| Key | Type | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `initial_node` | string | yes | Key of the node where every call starts |
| `nodes` | object | yes | Map of node key to node definition |
| `system_prompt` | string | no | Global rules. Part of the dialogue prompt in every node |
| `global_nodes` | object | no | Interrupt handlers that can fire from any node. See "Global nodes" |
| `test_variables` | object | no | Default values for call variables. See "Variables" |
| `context_variables` | object | no | A state block of chosen variables for the dialogue model. See "Context variables" |
| `tools` | array | no | Workflow-level lifecycle tools. See tools-and-code.md |
| `agent_config` | object | no | Model and call settings. See below |
| `nodePositions` | object | no | Layout for the visual editor. The working builder omits it |

**`agent_config`**: omit it. The platform fills in defaults. It holds model, voice and timeout settings that a builder for this event does not need. In a simulation you choose the models with the override fields described in api.md.

**No `null` values.** The schema is strict. Leave an optional field out, or set an optional string to `""`. A `null` fails validation.

The REST API takes the workflow inside a request body `{"name": "...", "workflow": {...}}`. The object described on this page is the value of `workflow`.

## Node types

| `node_type` | Purpose | Speaks to the user | Carries |
|---|---|---|---|
| `conversation` | A dialogue step | yes | `task_message`, `tools`, `extraction_schema`, `transitions` |
| `api_request` | Runs an HTTP call on entry | usually not | `pre_actions`, node-level `response_mapping`, `transitions` |
| `code` | Runs a Python snippet on entry | usually not | `pre_actions` with a `code_exec` function, `transitions` |
| `end_call` | Ends the call | optional farewell | `terminal` |

Other node types exist: `transfer_call`, `integration`, `knowledge_base`, `reschedule_call`, `invoke_agent`, `exit`. Telephony, voice settings, knowledge base and integrations also exist on the platform. You do not need any of them here and this page does not describe them.

The platform strips fields that do not belong to a node type, without an error:

- `tools` is kept only on `conversation` nodes.
- `pre_actions` is kept only on `api_request` and `code` nodes (and the other non-conversation action types).

So a node cannot have both. If a call must run before a conversation node, put it in its own `api_request` node in front.

## Node fields

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | | Node name. Use the same value as the node's key, in `snake_case` |
| `node_type` | string | | One of the types above |
| `task_message` | string | | The instruction for the dialogue model in this node |
| `role_message` | string | | Extra persona text for this node. Rarely needed |
| `on_enter` | object | `{"type": "llm"}` | What happens on entry. See "Entry behaviour" |
| `on_enter_first_entry_only` | boolean | `false` | Run the entry behaviour only on the first visit |
| `transitions` | array | | Outgoing transitions, in priority order |
| `routing_prompt` | string | | Extra context for the routing model in this node |
| `loop_condition` | string | | Intent description for staying in the node. See "Loop conditions" |
| `loop_prompt` | string | | Replaces `task_message` from the second turn in the node |
| `extraction_schema` | array | | Variables to extract from user speech in this node |
| `tools` | array | | Tools the dialogue model may call. `conversation` nodes only |
| `pre_actions` | array | | Calls the engine runs on entry. `api_request` and `code` nodes |
| `response_mapping` | array | | For `pre_actions` nodes: maps the call result to variables. Node level |
| `passthrough` | boolean | `false` | Route right after entry, without waiting for the user |
| `passthrough_default_transition` | string | | Target node for a passthrough node |
| `max_node_turns` | integer | `10` | Cap on user turns spent in the node |
| `max_turn_transition` | string | | Target node when the cap is reached |
| `terminal` | object | | The end-call function. `end_call` nodes only |
| `disable_inactivity_monitor` | boolean | `false` | Switch off silence check-ins for this node |
| `suppress_tool_results` | boolean | `false` | Hide raw call results from the dialogue model. See tools-and-code.md |
